partial_case.facts: The resident lives in a house with a shed in the garden. She complained about delays to repairs which caused a bedroom to be damp and cold, and delays in replacing external doors. On 25 April 2024, the resident raised 2 complaints: first, that she had reported problems with external doors in January 2024 with no response from the landlord; second, that a roof repair had been raised in November 2023 but no work started since an inspection in December 2023. The landlord sent its stage 1 response on 13 June 2024 acknowledging a 7-month delay and offering £200 compensation. On 20 June 2024, the resident escalated her complaints. On 2 July 2024, the landlord increased compensation offers to £450 for the roof leak and £275 for doors, plus £25 each for delayed responses. The landlord sent its stage 2 response on 9 September 2024, finding no roof faults but identifying brickwork needing repointing, scheduled for 30 September 2024. It increased compensation offers to £450 for doors, £450 for roof, £144 for energy reimbursement, and £150 for complaint handling.

key_reasoning_quotes.text: The landlord did not carry out inspections and repairs in line with its repairs policy. Jobs were left unresolved when it changed sub-contractors, leading to long delays.
The landlord's failure to accurately consider the financial detriment to the resident has caused her further distress and inconvenience.
While there were avoidable delays by the landlord in replacing the external doors, it recognised this in its response. It offered an apology and appropriate compensation to put matters right.

partial_case.facts: The resident lives in a house with a shed in the garden and complained about delays to repairs that caused a bedroom to be damp and cold, and about the time taken to replace external doors. On 25 April 2024 she raised two complaints: one about external doors reported in January 2024 and one about a roof repair raised in November 2023 with no work started after a December 2023 inspection. The landlord sent a stage 1 roof repair response on 13 June 2024, offering £200 compensation, and later reassessed compensation on 2 July 2024. On 9 September 2024 it sent its stage 2 response, stating that brickwork needed repointing, that an external door had been missed, and increasing offers to £450 for doors, £450 for roof, £144 for increased energy usage, and £150 for complaint handling. The resident referred the matter to the Ombudsman because work remained outstanding and she disputed the calculation of electricity reimbursement.

key_reasoning_quotes.text: The landlord did not carry out inspections and repairs in line with its repairs policy. Jobs were left unresolved when it changed sub-contractors, leading to long delays.
While there were avoidable delays by the landlord in replacing the external doors, it recognised this in its response. It offered an apology and appropriate compensation to put matters right.
While there were failings by the landlord in its complaint handling, it recognised this in its response and offered appropriate compensation and an apology.

The landlord’s calculation is therefore not appropriate. It failed to consider or respond to her suggested calculation, or consider her circumstances and the impact on her, missing the opportunity to put things right.

The landlord’s offer of compensation in relation to the delay to repairs was broadly reasonable. However, its failure to accurately consider the financial detriment to the resident has caused her further distress and inconvenience.
The landlord’s responses were significantly delayed at both stages, and it did not acknowledge the resident’s complaints, despite her chasing for acknowledgement several times.
